submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole marks specific, identifying particulars inside a noun phrase: it is most active on the leading token of an attributive quantity or ordinal ('a 500 MW plant', 'the 80,000-seater stadium', 'the 28th annual meeting', '3.34 million pounds building', '70.9 degrees of inclination') and on a name or demonym that names a specific entity ('the United States', 'the German team', 'the Yuzhnoye Design Bureau'), with a weaker response on the determiner that opens such a phrase ('the', 'its', usually right after a preposition). It is near zero on generic or vague description - vague quantifiers ('a very large plant', 'much capacity'), plain common-noun phrases ('in the country', 'the factory') and numerals used as a bare post-verbal count ('seats 80,000') - and on abstract, non-factual prose.

By the middle of the nineteenth century the town had changed almost beyond recognition. The river that had once turned the mills had silted up, and the mills themselves stood empty along the bank. Families who had worked them for generations drifted toward the cities, where the factories paid better wages and never asked about a man's father or where he had learned his trade. The council debated for years what should be done with the waterfront. Some wanted warehouses, others a park, and a few, remembering the old timber trade, wanted the wharves rebuilt exactly as they had been. Nothing was decided. The committee met, took evidence, adjourned, and met again in a different room under a different chairman.

Rain fell on the empty buildings for a decade. Children used the loading docks as a playground, and in winter the flooded cellars froze hard enough to skate on. The parish magazine recorded these small events faithfully: a roof collapsing, a chimney falling into the yard, the death of the last miller, who had insisted to the end that trade would return. His obituary ran long and mentioned no one else.

The turning point came from outside. A surveyor arrived one autumn, spent the season measuring the riverbed, and left without explaining himself. Months later a proposal was on the table: a new road along the north bank, a bridge at the old ford, and a row of houses where the timber yard had been. The council, exhausted by argument, approved it in a single evening. Work began the following spring.

The men who built the bridge came from all over the region, and they lodged in the town while the work lasted. Wages were poor, the hours long, and the accidents frequent, though the company disputed every claim. By the time the last span was lowered, the town had a grocer, a butcher, a schoolroom and a newspaper. The newspaper, predictably, was in favour of progress, and said so every week.

When the bridge opened, the ceremony was modest: a ribbon, a short speech by the mayor, and a brass band that had not rehearsed. Nobody thought much of it at the time. But the road brought traffic, and the traffic brought trade, and within a generation the waterfront that the committee had failed to save had been rebuilt several times over. The old photographs, kept in a drawer at the library, show a muddy lane, a few carts, and a crowd of a few hundred people gathered for the opening.

The town's population, which had fallen for a generation, began to rise again. New streets were laid out on the hill above the ford, and the names chosen for them recorded trades that no longer existed anywhere in the parish. The last of the old mill buildings was pulled down one spring, and its stones were used to face the new school.

Only one structure from that era survives largely unaltered. The cast-iron bridge that the Leeds engineers designed, with its 62-metre central span, still carries traffic today, though the road surface has been replaced twice and the railings once.
